messages.subject: Additional arrival when start_time is not zero
messages.subject_clean: Additional arrival when start_time is not zero
messages.body_plain:
Hi Iñaki,

First of all thank you so much for sharing Simmer with everyone, the package is great!

While trying to recover an experimentally observed arrival distribution (which changes according to the hour of the day), I noticed that the generators I was joining were having what looks like an additional event right before the 'start_time' int the 'from_to' function.  I tried reproducing the issue in this minimalistic example:

bank <-
  simmer() %>%
  add_generator("Customer",
                trajectory("Customer's path"),
                from_to(start_time = 0,
                        stop_time = 60,
                        arrive = FALSE,
                        dist = function() { -1 }))

bank %>% run() %>% get_mon_arrivals()

> [1] name          start_time    end_time      activity_time finished
> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

As expected, no arrivals take place. However, if start_time is larger than 0, there is one event right before start_time:

bank <-
  simmer() %>%
  add_generator("Customer",
                trajectory("Customer's path"),
                from_to(start_time = 10,
                        stop_time = 60,
                        arrive = FALSE,
                        dist = function() { -1 }))

bank %>% run() %>% get_mon_arrivals()

>        name start_time end_time activity_time finished replication
> 1 Customer0          9        9             0     TRUE           1

1. Is this a feature or a bug?
2. Is there a way to prevent it?  Currently I am joining 24 generators for each hour of the day, and get 23 additional arrivals, which compresses the dynamic range of the events I want to characterize.

Thank you!

Thanks for your response, Iñaki.

The need for a -1 to terminate a generator before it generates any arrivals comes when there are two or more generators joined consecutively in time. Let's say the first generator, gen1, has a low arrival rate and the second one, gen2, has a high arrival rate. If we always let one arrival from gen1 to take place, that arrival time will likely fall well within the gen2's [start_time, stop_time] range, potentially preempting many arrivals from the gen2.  To fix that, if an attempted arrival time from gen1 goes beyond start_time from gen2, I shut down gen1.

Does that make sense?

Here is the example:

set.seed(1)

interarrival_times_per_period <- c(300, 200, 3) # each period extends over 60 units
sim <- simmer()

inter_arrival_time <- function(period, env) {
  time_delta = rexp(1, 1/interarrival_times_per_period[period])
  print(paste("Period:", period, "tentative time_delta:", time_delta))
  mins_into_the_period = now(env) - period*60
  # terminate generator if tentative arrival is crosses into next generator's period
  ifelse(time_delta + mins_into_the_period > 60, -1, time_delta)
}

a <- map(1:length(interarrival_times_per_period),
         function(i) add_generator(sim, paste0("customer period", i),
                trajectory(),
                from_to(start_time = i*60,
                        stop_time = (i + 1)*60 - 1,
                        arrive = FALSE,
                        dist = function() { inter_arrival_time(i, sim) })))

sim %>% run() %>% get_mon_arrivals()

messages.body_plain:
Generators 'from', 'to' and 'from_to' are convenience functions to
start and/or stop the arrival process at specified times, so they are
not designed to cope with any -1 coming from the distribution
provided. Changing this behaviour complicates the design and does not
add any new functionality, so I think that the best solution is to add
a warning in the documentation about this.

Iñaki

messages.subject: Control of queueing behaviour by arrival?
messages.subject_clean: Control of queueing behaviour by arrival?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

 I'm still working on my hospital model - data now fully prepared and getting stuck into the r-simmer side of things.

 Is there any way to turn on and off queueing by arrival or during a seize activity? renege_in() doesn't seem to do quite what I want - though there may be a workaround I haven't thought of.

 My use case:

 Patient arrives in hospital and seizes a bed on the admission ward.

 I'd like them to try to seize a bed on the surgical ward, and enter a queue if one isn't immediately available. Once they successfully seize that, they'll release the admission ward bed and start a timeout for their stay.

 Once they're on the surgical ward, if they're dropped (either by pre-emption or reduction in capacity) I don't want them to enter the surgical ward's queue as a patient needs at least one bed seized at all times. (in this case they should "roll down" and seize a bed on a different - less appropriate - ward, which I'm expecting to use handle_unfinished for).

 I can't just reduce the surgical ward queue to zero because there will be other patients who need to seize a bed (but have one on the admissions ward so don't mind queueing)

 My current best-guess at a workaround is that in the event of a failed seize it's repeated every few hours, though this results in a fairly random queue.

 Does anyone have any better ideas?

thanks!

tom

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 17 May 2019 at 10:15, Tom Lawton <t...@t-lawton.org> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
>  I'm still working on my hospital model - data now fully prepared and
> getting stuck into the r-simmer side of things.
>
>  Is there any way to turn on and off queueing by arrival or during a
> seize activity? renege_in() doesn't seem to do quite what I want -
> though there may be a workaround I haven't thought of.

Not sure what you mean by "turning on and off queueing by arrival",
but note that you also have renege_if, which is basically the same as
renege_in, but based on a signal instead of a timeout.

>  My use case:
>
>  Patient arrives in hospital and seizes a bed on the admission ward.
>
>  I'd like them to try to seize a bed on the surgical ward, and enter a
> queue if one isn't immediately available. Once they successfully seize
> that, they'll release the admission ward bed and start a timeout for
> their stay.
>
>  Once they're on the surgical ward, if they're dropped (either by
> pre-emption or reduction in capacity) I don't want them to enter the
> surgical ward's queue as a patient needs at least one bed seized at
> all times. (in this case they should "roll down" and seize a bed on a
> different - less appropriate - ward, which I'm expecting to use
> handle_unfinished for).
>
>  I can't just reduce the surgical ward queue to zero because there
> will be other patients who need to seize a bed (but have one on the
> admissions ward so don't mind queueing)
>
>  My current best-guess at a workaround is that in the event of a
> failed seize it's repeated every few hours, though this results in a
> fairly random queue.
>
>  Does anyone have any better ideas?

You can do the following. You set the surgical ward queue to zero
initially, and set up a reject trajectory in that seize. In that
reject trajectory, you just increase the queue capacity in one unit
and retry (rollback to seize). Of course, when a patient seizes the
surgical ward, it decreases the queue capacity. In this way, the queue
size is always equal to the number of patients waiting.

What happens if a patient being served in the surgical ward gets
preempted for some reason? It is automatically dropped, because there
is no room in the queue according to our setup above, and it is
catched in handle_unfinished.

Does this make sense?

Iñaki

> I'm searching for potential business cases for simmer here in Finland.
> I suppose complex,  big data simulations would be good targets?

For sure, simmer allows you to simulate pretty complex scenarios (see
the vignettes [1], and especially the use cases in [2]). It's also
prepared for very big simulations: it's fast, and, although monitoring
is performed in memory by default, there's an interface to change
that. You can use, e.g., monitor_csv() to directly store the generated
data on disk; or monitor_dbi(), from the experimental package
simmer.mon [3], to store data on a database.

[1] https://r-simmer.org/articles/
[2] https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-aa-5g
[3] https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer.mon

Iñaki

messages.body_plain:
Thanks very much for the Bank Tutorial Part I and Part II. I found it very useful. I was trying to create a variant of the bank example as follows:
1. There two sets of customers (customers1 whose tasks are longer to process, and customers2 whose tasks are shorter to process).
2. There are 2 resources (a) Counter 1 that gives priority to customers1 and services customers2 only when no customer1 is in the queue (b) Counter 2 that services only customers2.

I couldn't figure out how to impose the logic above on resources. I would appreciate any thoughts you might have. Below is an example code that I created when customers1/counter 1 and customers2/counter 2 are independent of each other and just a few customers.

arrtime1 = 15
servicetime1 = 10

arrtime2 = 8
servicetime2 = 5

env = simmer()

cust1 = trajectory() %>%
        seize("counter1") %>%
        timeout(function() servicetime1) %>%
        release("counter1")

cust2 = trajectory() %>%
        seize("counter2") %>%
        timeout(function() servicetime2) %>%
        release("counter2")

env %>% add_resource("counter1", 1) %>%
        add_resource("counter2", 1) %>%
        add_generator("cust1", cust1, at(0)) %>%
        add_generator("cust2", cust2, at(0, 3)) %>%
        run(until = 100)

Thanks,
Shankar

messages.body_plain:
You need to implement a sort of token bucket for customer2 using an
additional resource:

library(simmer)

servicetime1 <- 5
servicetime2 <- 10

customer1 <- trajectory() %>%
  set_capacity("token", 1) %>%

  seize("counter1") %>%
  timeout(function() servicetime1) %>%

  release("counter1") %>%
  set_capacity("token", function() {
    if (get_queue_count(env, "counter1"))
      1
    else 2
  })

customer2 <- trajectory() %>%
  seize("token") %>%
  select(paste0("counter", 1:2), "first-available") %>%
  seize_selected() %>%
  timeout(function() {
    if (get_selected(env) == "counter1")
      servicetime1
    else servicetime2
  }) %>%
  release_selected() %>%
  release("token")

env <- simmer()
env %>%
  add_resource("token", 2) %>%
  add_resource("counter1") %>%
  add_resource("counter2") %>%
  add_generator("customer1", customer1, at(3, 8, 9)) %>%
  add_generator("customer2", customer2, at(0, 1, 2)) %>%
  run()

Note that this won't work if you run into simultaneous events in some
cases. If you use random distributions for arrival/service times, you
are safe.

Iñaki

The problem with your approach is that there may be customer2 arrivals
sitting in the queue of counter2 and then counter1 becomes available.
You would need some mechanism to exit that queue and try counter1
again. This could be implemented using renege_if and signals, but I
think it's more complicated than my approach.

Iñaki
